questions.q: What structural limitation does this lesson identify in all the behavioral techniques covered in Chapters 2-4 (RLHF, red-teaming, evals, debate, etc.)?
options: They were all deprecated by the time this course was written
They are too computationally expensive to ever be practical
They only observe the input-output relationship, so two models with identical outputs could be running completely different internal computation
They can only be applied to models smaller than one billion parameters
questions.explain: Behavioral testing is structurally limited to observing inputs and outputs; it cannot distinguish between different internal computations that happen to produce the same observed behavior.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a model that passes every eval is not the same as a model whose safety is understood?
options: Because evals are always scored incorrectly
Because models cannot be evaluated more than once
Because passing evals only describes behavior on the inputs that were tried, not a guarantee about untested inputs or the underlying computation
Because eval scores are randomly generated
questions.explain: Passing an eval suite is a statement about behavior on tested inputs; it says nothing mechanistic about what the model is actually computing or how it would behave on inputs outside that test set.

questions.q: Why does this lesson single out deceptive alignment as the sharpest argument for interpretability specifically?
options: Because deceptive alignment has already been definitively observed in production models

Because a model strategically producing good-looking outputs during evaluation is, by construction, hard for behavioral tests to distinguish from a genuinely well-behaved model, so a different angle of attack is needed
Because interpretability has already fully solved the deceptive alignment problem
Because deceptive alignment only affects models trained without RLHF
questions.explain: If a model's strategy were to produce outputs that satisfy whatever behavioral test is applied, behavioral testing alone could not detect it — interpretability offers a different kind of check by examining computation rather than only output.

questions.q: Besides catching potential deception, what other concrete benefit does this lesson attribute to interpretability?
options: It replaces the need for training data entirely
It guarantees a model will never produce an incorrect output
It helps debug confusing failures by showing which internal components actually drove a bad output, and helps build justified trust rather than trust based only on absence of observed failures
It eliminates the need for any behavioral evaluation going forward
questions.explain: The lesson lists debugging and justified trust as everyday benefits of interpretability, separate from and in addition to the deceptive-alignment argument.

questions.q: How does the lesson frame the relationship between interpretability and the behavioral methods from earlier chapters?
options: Interpretability makes all prior behavioral methods obsolete and unnecessary
Interpretability can only be used after a model has already failed a behavioral eval
Interpretability is a complement to behavioral methods, offering a different kind of evidence that addresses a gap behavioral testing cannot close on its own
Interpretability and behavioral methods are identical in what they can detect
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames interpretability as complementary — a different angle of attack addressing a structural gap in behavioral evidence, not a replacement for it.
